title: Living ashtpadi 21
hookLine: the vast and the quiet behind all things
tomorrow: Ashtpadi 22, salok: Lord of all beings

cards: Right before dawn, the sky does something odd. It isn't dark and it isn't light. It goes a deep, even gray-blue, and everything is very quiet: no birds yet, no traffic, the trees just shapes.
Then color comes in from one edge, a line of pale yellow, then pink, and all at once it's morning, and the noise of the day begins. In a small way, the twenty-first ashtpadi plays out every dawn.

teach.b: Here's the twenty-first ashtpadi in brief. Before anything, the Formless One, nirankaar, rested in sunn, the deep stillness: no form, no grudge, no joy or sorrow, only the One.
Then, by God's own will, the play began, and the world of forms spread out. Living that doesn't mean thinking about the beginning of the universe all day.
It means remembering that the stillness didn't go anywhere.
In Sikh teaching, the One who rested in sunn is the same One inside the play now, behind all things, the way the quiet gray sky is still there behind the sunrise.
That's one reason Sikh practice values amrit vela, the hours before dawn. In Japji, Guru Nanak names that ambrosial hour as the time to reflect on the greatness of the Name.

It's the time of day that looks most like the ashtpadi: quiet first, then the world. Sitting with the Name then is a way to meet the stillness before the noise begins, and carry a little of it into the noise.

teach.h: THE BUSY DAY IS NOT THE ENEMY.
teach.b: And the noise is not the enemy. Sikh teaching has no quarrel with the busy day; the Gurus worked, farmed, traded and led.
The point is that behind the busyness there's something vast and quiet the busyness can't touch. Some mornings it's easy to sense, and some mornings it isn't. Sukhmani says it's there either way.

how: Sikh practice values rising at amrit vela, the hours before dawn that Japji names as the time to reflect on the Name, for quiet remembrance before the day begins.

o: a God with no power over the world
the empty void left after the world ends
the Formless One, with no shape of its own

s: in Sikh teaching, the stillness ended when creation began
the One who rested in sunn is the same One behind all things now.
Japji names the ambrosial hour as the time to reflect on the Name
living ashtpadi 21 means avoiding busy work
the Gurus worked, farmed and led; the quiet sits behind the busyness.

games.q: you want to meet the stillness of ashtpadi 21 each day. when does Sikh practice point to?
o: whenever there's nothing else to do.
games.why: amrit vela. quiet first, then the world: the shape of the ashtpadi, every morning.

practice: Look at whatever sky is outside your window now, or, if you can't, remember a dawn you've seen, and let your breath be as slow as the sky changing.
Notice the quiet underneath the color, or underneath the light and noise of the day. If you pray, rest in Waheguru, behind all things.

wordCard.voice: Nirankaar, the Formless One: the stillness nirankaar rested in before creation is still here, behind the play; amrit vela, before dawn, is a daily way to meet it.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nirankaar, the Formless One, who rested in sunn before creation.

carryVoice: Your line: behind all things. Quiet first, then the world, and the quiet stays. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 21 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 290–291)
